newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Treasuries to better Bunds short term.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Treasuries to better Bunds short term.

text.p: U.S. government debt will outperform German bonds in the short term, analysts said on Monday, but whether the move will be due to gains by Treasuries or losses by Bunds is up for debate.
Whichever way investors look at it though, the 10-year T-note/Bund yield spread is set to target 50 basis points in the weeks ahead from 63 currently, analysts said.
"For the time being, Treasuries look good value," said Stuart Thomson at Nikko Europe in London. "We'll see a gentle outperformance of Treasuries relative to Germany."

Thomson, Nikko's chief international economist here, said scant economic data out this week will give Treasuries a technical boost as the flow of funds from Asia continues to rush into the U.S. market.

The U.S. presidentital election on November 5 was unlikely to cause much of stumbling block for Treasuries with incumbent Bill Clinton widely expected to trounce his Republican candidate Bob Dole and sweep to another four year term.
Meanwhile, the German debt market will cruise in neutral, said Thomson.
September M3 money supply data released earlier on Monday were in line with expecations with growth of 8.4 percent but remained outside the Bundesbank's four to seven percent target.
Monetary capital formation bounced back up in September but not enough to allow the Bundesbank to trim rates, Thomson said.

"M3 says it all," he said. "We don't expect the next move in German rates to come until after next year and these M3 fgirues brings home to the market that the opportunity the Bundesbank has to ease is extremely limited," he said.
Thomson expects the T-note/Bund spread to hit 55 basis points in the weeks ahead but to hurdle 50, markets need to be convinced the U.S. economy will slow down by the fourth quarter.

This is where Michale Burke, bond strategist at Citibank, differs. While Burke sees the spread heading for 50 basis points by the end of the year and to 25 by the second quarter of 1997, it will not be because of a U.S. slowdown and Treasuries' gains.
"As a general principle, I have never seen a slowdown that started with a housing boom," Burke said, referring to robust home sales.

New single-family home sales jumped 4.7 percent in August to a seasonally adjusted 832,000 units, the highest level since April 1986. An increase in durable goods purchases was sure to follow, pushing up already high consumption levels, he said.
The spread will move in Treasuries favour at the expense of Bunds, Burke said.
"The outlook over the medium term is that the German economy is likely to accelerate from a period of recession and slow growth at the end of this year and going into 1997," he said.
Burke said recent data showed the Germany economy has begun to recover. Export orders and exports, the September Ifo business climate index and investment have all turned up.

"Even private consumption is showing some signs of life based on moderate income growth of about four percent but also due to a rundown in savings as consumers become less concerned about impending tax hikes," he said.
Money supply may be slowing but Burke said it will have little impact either for the economy or policy, with the Bundesbank in the past moving interest rates regardless of M3.
Robert Prior, economist at James Capel in London, said however, some aspects of M3, pointed to a rocky recovery for Germany and he would opt for Bunds.

"I think the most encouraging aspect of it is the slowdown in bank lending growth. It may be heralding a slowdown in the pace of recovery in the next few months," he said. "That will be quite supportive of the German bond market."
